facts.statement: The genus Enchodus was first described by Louis Agassiz in 1835.
facts.quote: authority: Agassiz, 1835

facts.statement: Enchodus fossils range from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, with possible records from the Barremian and Paleogene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Albian-Maastrichtian~ Possible Barremian & Paleogene records

facts.statement: Enchodus species ranged from small to medium sizes, with the largest species, E. zinensis, reaching 172.2 cm in length.
facts.quote: Enchodus species were small to medium in size, with E. zinensis reaching 172.2 cm long.

facts.statement: Enchodus was a predatory species, indicated by its large fangs, sleek body, and large eyes.
facts.quote: These fangs, along with a long sleek body and large eyes, suggest Enchodus was a predatory species.

facts.statement: E. petrosus typically measured around 76.7 cm but could exceed 1 meter, and its fossils are common in formations like the Niobrara Chalk and Pierre Shale within the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: E. petrosus, with standard length around 76.7 cm and sometimes over 1 m, is known from common remains coming from the Niobrara Chalk, the Mooreville Chalk Formation, the Pierre Shale, and other geological formations deposited within the Western Interior Seaway and the Mississippi Embayment.

facts.statement: Large E. petrosus individuals had fangs over 6 cm long, giving their skulls a resemblance to modern deep-sea fishes like anglerfish and viperfish.
facts.quote: Large individuals of this species had fangs measuring over 6 cm in length, giving its skull an appearance somewhat reminiscent of modern deep-sea fishes, such as anglerfish and viperfish.

facts.statement: Some Enchodus species, like E. parvus, were very small, measuring only a few inches in length.
facts.quote: Other species, such as E. parvus, were considerably smaller, measuring only some centimetres (a few inches) long.

facts.statement: Enchodus remains are frequently found in the stomach contents of larger predators such as sharks, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and the seabird Baptornis advenus.
facts.quote: Despite being a formidable predator, remains of Enchodus are commonly found among the stomach contents of larger predators, including sharks, other bony fish, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and seabirds such as Baptornis advenus.

facts.statement: Enchodus fossils have been discovered worldwide.
facts.quote: Enchodus fossils have been found all over the world.

facts.statement: The potentially latest Enchodus remains are from the earliest Eocene of Barmer, India.
facts.quote: Potentially the latest Enchodus remains are known from the earliest Eocene of Barmer, India.

facts.statement: It is debated whether post-Cretaceous Enchodus records represent actual survival or are merely reworked Cretaceous material.
facts.quote: However, it has also been suggested that all post-Cretaceous Enchodus records are just reworked material.

facts.statement: Enchodus species are generally classified into two clades: North American and Mediterranean.
facts.quote: Species of Enchodus are generally classified into two different clades, the North American and the Mediterranean.

facts.statement: The earliest known Enchodus species is E. zimapanensis, found in the late Albian-aged El Doctor Formation of Mexico.
facts.quote: The earliest known species is E. zimapanensis from the late Albian-aged El Doctor Formation of Mexico.

facts.statement: Potentially earlier Enchodus remains from the late Barremian/early Aptian of Brazil exist, but they are too fragmentary to be confidently assigned to the genus.
facts.quote: Potentially earlier remains are known from the late Barremian/early Aptian of Brazil (Morro de Chaves Formation), but these specimens are too fragmentary to confidently assign to this genus.

facts.statement: The genus Enchodus was first described by Agassiz in 1835.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Agassiz, 1835

facts.statement: Enchodus belongs to the family Enchodontidae.
facts.quote: familia: Enchodontidae

facts.statement: Species of Enchodus ranged from small to medium size.

facts.statement: The species E. zinensis could reach a length of 172.2 cm (67.8 inches).

facts.statement: A notable feature of the genus was the large fangs located on the front of the upper and lower jaws and on the palatine bones.
facts.quote: Uno de los atributos más notables del género son los grandes colmillos en la parte frontal de las mandíbulas superior e inferior y en los huesos palatinos

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Enchodus was a predatory species based on its large fangs, long slender body, and large eyes.
facts.quote: Estos colmillos, junto con un cuerpo largo y esbelto y ojos grandes, sugieren que Enchodus era una especie depredadora

facts.statement: E. petrosus had a standard length of around 76.7 cm (30.2 inches) and occasionally exceeded 1 meter (3 feet 3 inches).
facts.quote: E. petrosus, con una longitud estándar de alrededor de 76,7 cm (30,2 pulgadas) y, en ocasiones, de más de 1 m (3 pies 3 pulgadas)

facts.statement: Large specimens of E. petrosus possessed fangs longer than 6 cm (2.4 inches).
facts.quote: Los ejemplares grandes de esta especie tenían colmillos de más de 6 cm (2,4 pulgadas) de longitud

facts.statement: Other species, such as E. parvus, were considerably smaller, measuring only a few centimeters (a few inches) in length.
facts.quote: Otras especies, como E. parvus, eran considerablemente más pequeñas, midiendo solo algunos cm (unas pocas pulgadas) de longitud

facts.statement: Enchodus lived from the Callovian to the Burdigalian, spanning 165.3 to 15.98 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Callovian to Burdigalian (165.3 to 15.98 million years ago)

facts.statement: Fossils of Enchodus have been found worldwide.
facts.quote: Se han encontrado fósiles de Enchodus en todo el mundo

facts.statement: The potentially most recent remains of Enchodus are known from the early Eocene of Barmer, India.

facts.statement: It is debated whether all post-Cretaceous records of Enchodus are merely reworked material.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, también se ha sugerido que todos los registros posteriores al Cretácico son solo material reelaborado

facts.statement: In 2026, Nelson, Murray, and Brinkman described fossil material of E. petrosus and E. cf. gladiolus from the Upper Cretaceous Bearpaw Formation in Alberta, Canada, including the largest articulated skull of the genus reported to date.
facts.quote: Fossil material of two members of the genus Enchodus (E. petrosus and E. cf. gladiolus), including the largest articulated skull of a member of the genus reported to date, is described from the Upper Cretaceous Bearpaw Formation (Alberta, Canada) by Nelson, Murray & Brinkman (2026)
